title: Marguerite and the Static
premise: Bram Amberdale, a xenolinguist turned cargo hauler, is conscripted to interpret the impossible: a survey ship, the Meridian, has returned from deep space with its crew biologically aged backward into childhood. The ship's logs reveal a temporal anomaly and a terrible arithmetic — the station's failing cryo-banks can wake only half the colony's sleepers before power collapses. As Bram decodes the children's fractured transmissions, he discovers they carry a warning encoded in a language only his altered mind can parse: the anomaly is drifting toward the station itself. He falls in love with Wren, a Meridian engineer de-aged to nineteen with no memory of their past marriage, and must choose between spending the last cryo-power saving her or preserving enough sleepers to evacuate everyone when the anomaly arrives. In the end Bram sacrifices the Meridian's data core — and his own chance at escape — to broadcast the warning in time, waking the full colony; Wren, choosing him over her restored memories, stays as the anomaly's edge touches the hull, and the two step into the static together, alive because love proved a better algorithm than duty.
about_author: Oscar Amberdale is the pen name of a former orbital logistics dispatcher who spent nine years writing radio plays for long-haul crews. Marguerite and the Static is their second novel, written aboard a decommissioned freighter now moored off the coast of Newfoundland.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Quiet
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Establishes his cargo route through contested orbits, his linguistic dreams turning alien, and his estrangement from the colony he once served. He receives an emergency priority summons he cannot refuse. Emotional beat: weary isolation cracked open by obligation.

chapters.title: The Ship That Came Home Young
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. He docks at Kepler Station and sees the Meridian — crewed by children in adult uniforms, running on instinct and muscle memory. Station command quarantines the ship and demands answers. Emotional beat: uncanny dread tempered by tenderness.

chapters.title: Marguerite
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Among the de-aged crew is a girl of about six who hums a lullaby only Bram's grandmother knew — a song that shouldn't exist out here. Command names her the anomaly's key witness. Emotional beat: grief surfacing as wonder.

chapters.title: Wren at Nineteen
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The Meridian's chief engineer wakes physically nineteen, married to a stranger she doesn't remember. She studies Bram across the quarantine glass, cataloguing him like a system she once maintained. Emotional beat: disorientation sharpening into defiant curiosity.

chapters.title: A Grammar of Backward Time
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. He begins decoding the children's speech, which is accreted with fragments of an alien syntax — language flowing in reverse tense. His altered dreams suddenly make sense: something taught him years ago. Emotional beat: exhilaration shadowed by violation.

chapters.title: Half the Sleepers
chapters.summary: Commander Ilsa Voss's POV. The station's cryo-banks are failing; power audits confirm only half the colony's twelve thousand sleepers can be woken safely. Voss drafts triage criteria and asks Bram to keep it quiet. Emotional beat: cold duty calcifying around guilt.

chapters.title: What the Children Remember
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Interviewing the de-aged crew, Bram learns they remember their whole lives — compressed, dreamlike, told in the wrong order. Marguerite draws the anomaly: a spiral eating its own tail. Emotional beat: compassion deepening into resolve.

chapters.title: Muscle Memory
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren repairs a coolant line she has no conscious memory of learning to fix, then finds her own wedding ring fused inside a panel she welded years ago. She confronts Bram with it. Emotional beat: the past asserting itself against erasure.

chapters.title: The Triage List
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The list leaks. The station fractures into factions — families against singles, young against old. Bram realizes Wren's name sits below the cutoff line. Emotional beat: moral vertigo.

chapters.title: Static Between Us
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren and Bram work late shifts decoding together, building something new between them that neither the marriage nor the amnesia authorized. She tells him she won't be saved out of guilt. Emotional beat: intimacy kindled in honest friction.

chapters.title: The Spiral Moves
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Long-range sensors confirm the anomaly has left the Meridian's old coordinates and is drifting toward Kepler Station. Arrival window: eleven months. The triage debate becomes an evacuation problem. Emotional beat: dread converting abstraction into countdown.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Warning
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Marguerite, half-asleep, recites a full transmission in the reversed grammar: the anomaly isn't random — it responds to mass, to minds, to attention. Something in it is listening. Emotional beat: terror reframed as contact.

chapters.title: Committee of the Waking
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs in interlocking scenes. A raucous station assembly debates who wakes first. Bram publicly breaks with Voss, arguing the list is a lie of arithmetic, not necessity. Emotional beat: found family forming in opposition.

chapters.title: The Engineer's Proof
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren proves the cryo-banks can be reconfigured to wake everyone — if someone reroutes power manually during the final surge, a suicide posting. She volunteers herself. Emotional beat: love declared as sacrifice.

chapters.title: Bram Refuses
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram refuses to let her die alone and instead proposes the unthinkable: use the Meridian's data core as bait, broadcasting continuously to draw the anomaly's attention away while the surge runs. Voss calls it madness. Emotional beat: stubborn hope against institutional despair.

chapters.title: What the Static Wants
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, dream-interleaved. In a shared lucid dream induced by the reversed grammar, Bram speaks with the anomaly directly: it is not devouring, it is unmaking time to survive its own death, and it is lonely. Emotional beat: awe dissolving fear into pity.

chapters.title: Eleven Days
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. With arrival imminent, Voss authorizes the plan but hedges — secretly keeping the original triage list loaded in case the surge fails. Bram discovers the betrayal. Emotional beat: trust breaking under pressure.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Aboard the Meridian, Bram transmits the entire decoded corpus — every child's memory, every reversed sentence — into the static. The anomaly slows, turns, listens. Marguerite, beside him, sings the lullaby. Emotional beat: climax of communion.

chapters.title: Surge
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. During the distraction, Wren rides the manual reroute as the cryo-banks fire in cascading waves. Systems burn around her; she holds the line past all rated tolerances. Every sleeper wakes. Emotional beat: triumph purchased with blood.

chapters.title: The Edge of the Hull
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The anomaly's boundary reaches the station. Instead of destruction, it passes through like weather — taking only what was offered: the Meridian's core, and the years the children lost, returned to them as they age forward again. Emotional beat: release after white-knuckle terror.

chapters.title: Two Names for One Life
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Restored to her true age, Wren holds both selves — the woman who married Bram and the nineteen-year-old who chose him again. She chooses, deliberately, both. They stand watch together as the colony rebuilds. Emotional beat: reconciliation without erasure.

chapters.title: Dreaming in Human Again
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, epilogue. Months later, Bram dreams in English for the first time in twelve years — but keeps one alien word, the anomaly's name for 'stay.' Marguerite, aging normally now, calls him family. The static is gone; the listening remains. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace.
